node.label: Deborah Cohen
node.date_label: The War Come Home (2001) · Comparison and History, co-edited (2004) · Household Gods (2006) · Family Secrets (2013)
node.description: Deborah Cohen argues in Household Gods: The British and their Possessions (2006) that religious values helped make domestic consumption respectable and that possessions became a means of expressing individuality. In Family Secrets (2013), she traces the changing relationship between secrecy and privacy in British families, showing how everyday negotiations could change social norms. Both books won the American Historical Association's Forkosch Prize. In the 2014 History Workshop roundtable, Matt Houlbrook praised Family Secrets' intellectual reach but questioned whether histories built from revealed secrets can capture those that never become visible. Her methodological essay ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001) examines the explanatory costs of comparison, including the difficulty of separating causes from context. With Peter Mandler, she challenged the evidence and claims about historical scale and public relevance in Jo Guldi and David Armitage's The History Manifesto in 2015.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The War Come Home: Disabled Veterans in Britain and Germany, 1914–1939 (2001); Comparison and History: Europe in Cross-National Perspective (2004), co-edited with Maura O'Connor; Household Gods: The British and their Possessions (2006); Family Secrets (2013); ‘The History Manifesto: A Critique’ (2015), with Peter Mandler; Last Call at the Hotel Imperial: The Reporters Who Took on a World at War (2022).
node.scope_note: Complete 2001 comparative-history essay and two 2014 roundtable contributions read. Household Gods is represented through its publisher description; Family Secrets through named readers. Other selected books were not read in full. Only the public opening of the 2015 critique and the indexed opening acknowledgment of The War Come Home were read; the reply and rejoinder remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas Laqueur was one of Deborah Cohen’s doctoral advisers (Berkeley PhD, 1996), as she acknowledges in The War Come Home (2001), alongside Gerald Feldman.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The publisher’s indexed acknowledgments extract names Laqueur and Feldman as advisers and distinguishes the other dissertation committee members. Cohen’s Northwestern CV, p. 1, Education, confirms the Berkeley history PhD in 1996. This records supervision only, with no claim of sole supervision or doctrinal influence.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Comparative History: Buyer Beware” (2001), Cohen uses Susan Pedersen’s Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993) as an example of comparison generating a new historical interpretation. Cohen, Guy Ortolano and Pedersen also coauthored “Peter and the special relationship” (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Cohen’s 2001 essay, printed p. 29, paragraph beginning “Let me offer two principal reasons to compare,” and note 11 on printed p. 32. The discussion uses Pedersen’s British/French family-allowance comparison as an example of a productive research question; Pedersen’s book remains unread. The 2025 coauthorship is confirmed by the publisher’s contents and indexed Interlude B byline. The War Come Home acknowledgments also credit Pedersen with inspiration and manuscript criticism, but those thanks do not carry or count toward this edge. Direction applies to the 2001 intellectual resource; the folded coauthorship is a separate, undirected witness.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen challenges the confidence in comparative method expressed in Bloch's 1928 essay.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, pp. 27, 30–31; notes 1, 27–28 distinguish 1928 original from 1953 English reprint. ‘technical instrument’ is the contested promise; Bloch's essay unread separately.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen uses Maier's Recasting Bourgeois Europe (1975) to show that comparative history can also be cross-national.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, p. 24, note 9: ‘maybe the best’. Maier's monograph unread; specific approving methodological example only.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Peter Mandler in ‘The History Manifesto: A Critique’ (2015), Cohen disputes Armitage and Jo Guldi's evidence for historians' retreat from long time spans and their proposed link between temporal scale and public significance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher opening extract, paragraphs 2–4 on p. 530, especially ‘What we object to’ and ‘This is true’. Joint credit retained on both sides; quantitative and digital methods are expressly accepted. Remainder of critique, 2014 book and reply unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Household Gods (2006), Cohen connects British domestic consumption with religious values and the use of possessions to express individuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Yale description, paragraphs 1–3: ‘religious fervor’ and ‘expressing individuality’. Publisher summary only; full book unread. Original year comes from CV, not the page's 2009 paperback date.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Family Secrets (2013), Cohen makes changing relations between privacy and secrecy part of the explanation of modern British family life, as Claire Langhamer emphasizes in her 2014 roundtable response.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Langhamer, complete contribution, paragraphs 1–5, particularly final two: ‘driver of change’. Mediated reading supports family history, not demographic measurement or a linear progress thesis; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen questions whether isolating variables adequately explains national differences in comparative historical sociology.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, pp. 27–28, beginning ‘In its search for causes’ and ‘If similar phenomena’: ‘generalizing’ explanations are qualified, not comparison abandoned. She applies the difficulty to her own book as well.

proposed_edges.relationship: Deborah Cohen's Family Secrets (2013) supplies an analysis of secrecy and privacy that Jennifer Crane explicitly extends to the medical history of child abuse and diagnostic radiology in her 2015 article on the battered child syndrome.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's open article, including the introduction and concluding application of Cohen. Crane names Family Secrets (2013) immediately after the supporting phrase and uses its separation of secrecy from privacy to frame the recognition of child abuse. This records a documented conceptual resource for medical history, not a claim that Cohen researched diagnostic radiology. Crane has no eligible person endpoint, so no person edge is proposed. Cohen's book was not read in full.

row.context: Studies the changing place of secrecy and privacy in modern British family life; Langhamer emphasizes everyday negotiations as a source of social change.
Questions the separation of causal variables from context in national comparisons while retaining comparison's explanatory possibilities.
Connects domestic consumer desires with religious values and the expression of individuality through possessions.
